title: Check yourself: results of a RecursiveTask

questions.stem: A log analyser counts error lines per service with a RecursiveTask on a ForkJoinPool. Its leaves call counts.merge(service, 1, Integer::sum) on a ConcurrentHashMap held in a field of the LogAnalyser, and analyse(file) clears that map before it invokes the root task and returns the map afterwards. One LogAnalyser serves the whole service. The counts are exact in every test, but in production a file analysed while another one is being analysed sometimes shows more errors than it has lines. What explains it?

options.text: The root task's join() hands back the map before every leaf has counted into it, so the caller reads counts that later grow
options.says: join() returns only once the task's compute() has returned, after it has joined its own halves; counts that are too high come from another file's leaves

options.text: The root task's join() hands back the map before its forked halves are joined, so their leaves add to it after the read
options.says: join() returns only once the task's compute() has returned, which is after it has joined its own halves; the counts are exact in every test

options.text: The map belongs to the analyser rather than to one call, so the leaves of both files count into it and one file's result holds the other's counts too
options.says: a thread-safe field fixes the arithmetic but not the ownership: two runs at once add into the same field

options.text: The map belongs to the analyser rather than to one call, so ConcurrentHashMap.merge on it counts some lines twice when the leaves of both files count one service at once
options.says: the page says a ConcurrentHashMap held by the report object adds correctly; the problem is that two runs share it

origin.section: A Task Returns Its Part of the Answer; Tasks That Write into Shared State Lose It

questions.stem: A monitoring job computes the median response time of a day's requests with a RecursiveTask<Double>. A leaf sorts its range and returns its median; a parent returns the average of the two medians it gets back. With a threshold of 100,000 the dashboard showed 182 ms; after the threshold was lowered to 1,000 it shows 171 ms, for the same day. Which change makes the result the day's median, whatever the threshold?

options.text: Return each range's median with its count and weight the two by count in the parent, since a median needs the size of both halves
options.says: no weighting of two medians gives the median of both halves; a median needs the values themselves

options.text: Return each range's values in sorted order and merge the two lists in the parent, since a median needs every value of both halves
options.says: the value a task returns must hold enough to combine with its sibling's so that any split gives the answer one task would

options.text: Keep returning medians but raise the threshold back to 100,000, since larger leaves give medians closer to the day's
options.says: the answer would still depend on the threshold; only one task for the whole day gives the true median this way

options.text: Keep returning medians but split at the median value instead of the middle index, since equal halves then average correctly
options.says: averaging two medians is wrong whatever the split; the combine needs more than two numbers

origin.section: The Parent Can Only Combine What Its Halves Return

questions.stem: A pricing job runs pool.invoke(root) on a ForkJoinPool(16). One leaf throws new IllegalStateException("no rate for EUR/TRY"). The job catches IllegalStateException e and logs e.getMessage(), which reads: java.lang.IllegalStateException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: no rate for EUR/TRY. Where do the two prefixes come from?

options.text: The failure was thrown once and logged by each of the two parent tasks it passed through on its way up to the root task
options.says: the prefixes are in the message of the exception the job caught: each thread the failure crossed built a copy whose message is the previous one's toString()

options.text: The failure was copied at each of two parent tasks it passed, each copy of the same class naming the one inside it
options.says: copies are made per thread the failure crossed, when the joining thread isn't the one that failed, not per parent task; parents on the thread that failed add no copy

options.text: The failure was thrown by three leaves, one with the rate's message and two that failed after reading the first one's message
options.says: one leaf threw; the chain is that one failure copied once per thread it crossed

options.text: The failure was copied on each of two threads it reached, each copy of the same class naming the one inside it
options.says: a joining thread that isn't the one that threw gets a new exception of the same class, built through its Throwable constructor, so its message is the original's toString(); each thread crossed adds one

origin.section: A Subtask's Exception Reaches join() as a Copy, and Its Siblings Keep Running

questions.stem: A validation job checks 30 million records with a RecursiveTask on its own ForkJoinPool. When the caller catches the first failure from invoke(), it calls cancel(true) on the root task, then reports. The report appears at once, but the pool's CPUs stay busy for about as long as a full validation. What keeps them busy?

options.text: Subtasks forked before the failure keep running, since cancelling the root neither takes them off the queues nor interrupts them
options.says: nothing cancels a task's siblings; the parent that threw never joined its forked half, and cancel's argument has no effect in a RecursiveTask

options.text: Subtasks forked before the failure keep running, since cancel(true) interrupts the root alone and neither dequeues nor interrupts its subtasks
options.says: in a RecursiveTask the argument of cancel has no effect and no task is interrupted, the root included; the subtasks run because nothing cancels a task's siblings

options.text: The pool retries the failed subtask on each worker in turn, since a record that fails on one worker may pass on another
options.says: the pool doesn't run a failed task again: it stays failed, and its exception goes to whoever joins it

options.text: The pool retries the failed subtask until the caller joins it, since a failure isn't final before someone has seen it
options.says: the pool doesn't run a failed task again: it stays failed, and joining it only reports the exception

origin.section: A Subtask's Exception Reaches join() as a Copy, and Its Siblings Keep Running

questions.stem: A puzzle service counts the ways to climb a staircase of n steps, one or two steps at a time, with a RecursiveTask: ways(n) forks ways(n - 1), computes ways(n - 2) and adds them, and below a cutoff of 25 it calls the same recursion on one thread. For 60 steps it runs for minutes on a 32-core ForkJoinPool. Which change helps most?

options.text: Lower the cutoff to 5 and keep the tasks, since many more tasks keep all 32 cores busy to the end
options.says: a task per call multiplies the task count and was slower than one thread on the page; the work stays exponential

options.text: Raise the cutoff to 45 and keep the tasks, since far fewer tasks cost less to create and queue
options.says: below the cutoff the same exponential recursion runs; fewer tasks don't remove the repeated work

options.text: Compute ways(1) up to ways(60) in one loop, each from the two before it, since the split repeats its subproblems
options.says: the subproblems of the split overlap; workers can only share repeated work, and a loop does about 60 additions

options.text: Compute ways(1) up to ways(60) in a parallel stream, one per worker, since the values don't depend on each other
options.says: each value needs the two before it, so the loop can't be split; and the loop already takes about 60 additions

origin.section: Splitting Shares the Work Among Workers; It Can't Remove Work the Recursion Repeats
